extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Plato, moral/political philosophers, and writers interested in education and literary censorship
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for composing or censoring literature, music, and education for youth in a moral/political pedagogy inspired by Plato's Republic; covers portrayal of gods/heroes, narrative style, music, visual arts, and physical education. Useful for writers, educators, and critics who design cultural materials for civic formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship of nursery tales
rubrics_metrics.description: Children ought not to learn what they will have to unlearn when they grow up; we must therefore have a censorship of nursery tales, banishing some and keeping others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ban stories that are 'improper' or 'immoral' (examples: parts of Homer and Hesiod). Young minds are impressionable and incapable of understanding allegory, so tales that depict immoral behaviour by gods or heroes should be suppressed or only allowed later in mystery rites.

rubrics_metrics.name: God must be represented as author of good only
rubrics_metrics.description: This is our first and great principle—God is the author of good only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow poets to depict the gods as causing evil or sin (e.g., blaming the gods for Niobe, Pelops, or the Trojan war); such representations are 'wicked, suicidal fiction' and must be forbidden to all, old or young.

rubrics_metrics.name: God is unchangeable/true
rubrics_metrics.description: With God is no variableness or change of form... He remains for ever fairest and best in his own image. This is our second great principle—God is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ban portrayals of gods taking disguises, begging in priestly guise, deceiving or changing form, or otherwise exhibiting changeability or falsehood; such depictions are blasphemous and corrupting for youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit depictions of gods/heroes with moral weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: We will not suffer the poets to say that [God] is the steward of good and evil... or that he makes men sin when he wishes to destroy them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbid narratives that show gods as jealous, deceitful, cowardly, or lamenting like humans (examples: Achilles weeping; Zeus lamenting). Such portrayals might encourage imitation of vice or weakness in citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'lie in the soul' (deep moral falsehood)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lie in the soul is a true lie, the corruption of the highest truth, the deception of the highest part of the soul, from which he who is deceived has no power of delivering himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject doctrines or assertions that fundamentally pervert moral truth (examples: 'being is becoming', 'knowledge is sensation', 'might is right'). These are worse than mere verbal falsehood and must be guarded against in education and literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish permissible 'lie in words' from dangerous 'lie in the soul'
rubrics_metrics.description: The lie in words is only such a deception as may occur in a play or poem, or allegory... which though useless to the gods may be useful to men in certain cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow figurative or allegorical falsehoods as pedagogical devices only when they have a good moral effect; reserve such use as a privilege of rulers for great objects, not for common persons to lie to rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purge tales that produce fear and cowardice
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another motive in purifying religion, which is to banish fear; for no man can be courageous who is afraid of death, or who believes the tales which are repeated by the poets concerning the world below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expunge passages that depict the afterlife as terrifying or encourage excessive lamentation (examples: Homeric terrors of Cocytus, Styx, shadowy souls). Such material is unsuitable for soldiers and guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance: self-control and obedience to authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Our youth must be temperate, and temperance consists in self-control and obedience to authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude literature that praises drunkenness, gluttony, immoderate sexual exploits, or other excesses; encourage examples of endurance and moderation ('Endure, my soul, thou hast endured worse').

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid praise or modelling of bribery and meanness
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither must we allow our citizens to receive bribes, or to say, 'Gifts persuade the gods, gifts reverend kings'; or to applaud ignoble advice to seek money before duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censor poems or stories that present corruption, bribery, greed or the profiteering of heroes as acceptable or admirable (examples: Phoenix advising Achilles to take money; Achilles accepting gifts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit depiction of cruel/meanness-as-virtue in heroes
rubrics_metrics.description: Such a combination of meanness and cruelty in Cheiron’s pupil [Achilles] is inconceivable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove or condemn scenes where heroes commit gratuitous cruelty (e.g., dragging Hector's body) or where cruelty is normalized; avoid presenting such acts as heroic models.

rubrics_metrics.name: One man plays one part only; limit imitation by guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: One man cannot in his life play many parts... as our guardians have their own business already... they will have enough to do without imitating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage guardians from acting/imitating multiple social roles (actors playing women, slaves, bullies, etc.). Imitation risks shaping identity ('the mask may become his face'); prefer stable role models and descriptive narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: If imitation allowed, imitate only the good
rubrics_metrics.description: If they imitate they should imitate, not any meanness or baseness, but the good only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any dramatic or imitative content admitted into civic education must only present noble, temperate, and courageous actions and characters; degrade or comic roles (slaves, cowards, sexual exaggeration) are forbidden for guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer descriptive/narrative style over imitative drama for guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: A good or wise man will be willing to perform good and wise actions, but he will be ashamed to play an inferior part... and he will prefer to employ the descriptive style with as little imitation as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrative/descriptive modes that present actions and their moral quality without theatrical imitation that could encourage role adoption; limit polyphonic/complex dramatic forms in civic education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity in music and instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Two remain—the Dorian and Phrygian... And as we reject varieties of harmony, we shall also reject the many-stringed, variously-shaped instruments which give utterance to them, and in particular the flute, which is more complex than any of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purge complex/mixed harmonies (Lydian, Ionian, mixed Lydian) and complex instruments; permit simple harmonies and instruments (Dorian for war, Phrygian for peace; lyre and harp in town; Pan’s-pipe in the fields). Music must foster temperance and courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match metre and style to subject; favour simple rhythms
rubrics_metrics.description: The style is to conform to the subject and the metre to the style... the simplicity and harmony of the soul should be reflected in them all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metres and rhythmic patterns appropriate to subject matter; prefer simple, balanced metres (martial measures, dactylic, trochaic, iambic arranged to equalize syllables) that instil harmony in the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual arts must conform to simplicity and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture and painting equally with music must conform to the law of simplicity... He who violates it cannot be allowed to work in our city, and to corrupt the taste of our citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbid images of deformity or unseemliness which might 'poison and corrupt' souls; cultivate a landscape of health and beauty so guardians internalize harmonious influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational sequence: imagination before reason
rubrics_metrics.description: A child must be trained in falsehood first and in truth afterwards... children must be taught through the medium of imagination as well as reason; their minds can only develope gradually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin education with stories and imaginative forms appropriate to the child's stage, then progressively introduce rational explanations and truths once capacities mature; avoid premature exposure to complex allegory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music of the soul: early musical training shapes moral character
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a music of the soul which answers to the harmony of the world; and the fairest object of a musical soul is the fair mind in the fair body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize musical education early in life to instill sense of beauty, temperance, and harmony; musical influences prepare the soul to welcome reason later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of falsehood reserved to rulers as 'medicine'
rubrics_metrics.description: This employment of falsehood must remain a privilege of state; the common man must not in return tell a lie to the ruler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow rulers to employ 'economies' or beneficial fictions for great objects when necessary, but tightly restrict this practice and prevent it from becoming general license for deceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gymnastics and diet suited to guardians: simplicity and endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: The guardians must abstain from strong drink... they will require a simpler kind of gymnastic, akin to their simple music; and for their diet a rule may be found in Homer, who feeds his heroes on roast meat only... Sicilian cookery and Attic confections... must be forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design physical education to produce alert, hardy soldiers (wide-awake and inured to changes of food/climate); forbid luxury foods and overindulgence that create dependency on doctors and lawyers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid luxury and excessive specialization that provoke war and social vice
rubrics_metrics.description: If we add hired servants the State will be complete... To feed all these superfluous mouths we shall need a part of our neighbour’s land, and they will want a part of ours. And this is the origin of war... luxury is the source [of disorders].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit luxury and unnecessary arts in the civic design to reduce envy, resource pressure, and the incentives to war; restrict roles (minimize parasitic occupations) to sustain civic justice and stability.
